THE NINES
99%     → 3.7 days down / year
99.9%   → 8.8 hours
99.99%  → 53 minutes
99.999% → 5 minutes
⚠ in a chain: 0.999³ = 99.7%

detect: 3 missed health checks   10 s

meta.title: Redundancy & Failover
meta.summary: Everything fails eventually. Design so that no single failure takes you down.

goals.text: Find and remove single points of failure

steps.title: How available is one of everything?
steps.body:
A simple stack: a load balancer, an app server and a database. Each one is up 99.9% of the time — that sounds great.

But a request needs **all three** working, so their availabilities multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ **99.7%**. That’s about 26 hours of downtime a year.

callout.text: Availability is usually quoted in “nines”. Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by 10×.

steps.title: Every box is a single point of failure
steps.body:
A [[single point of failure]] (SPOF) is anything whose failure alone takes the system down. Here, that’s every component.

A bad disk, a kernel panic, a botched deploy — any one of them and a million users see an error page.

callout.text: Hardware fails, software crashes and people make mistakes. Assume each will happen — the question is what breaks when it does.

steps.title: Redundancy: two of everything
steps.body:
Add a spare for each part: the load balancer runs as an active–passive pair, two app servers share traffic, and the database has a follower ready to take over.

Now *both* copies must fail at once for an outage — 0.1% × 0.1% = 0.0001%. Losing any single machine is a non-event.

callout.text: On paper, parts in parallel multiply their failure chances: two 99.9% copies give 99.9999%. Real pairs do worse — failover takes time, and both copies still share a building, a network and your deploys — so we count a cautious 99.95%.

steps.title: Copies that fail together
steps.body:
All those copies sit in one data center. Then a power outage (or a flood, a fibre cut, a cooling failure) takes out the whole building — and every “redundant” copy with it.

Failures that hit many components at once are [[correlated failures]]. Redundancy only helps if the copies fail *independently*.

callout.text: Shared power, network, racks, software versions and even the same bad config push can all take out every copy together.

steps.title: Spread across availability zones
steps.body:
Cloud regions are split into [[availability zones]]: separate data centers, kilometres to tens of kilometres apart, with their own power and network, joined by fast links.

Put one app server and one database copy in each zone. A zone-wide disaster now takes out only half.

callout.text: Same idea at every scale: spread across racks, zones and — for the most critical systems — whole regions.

changes: ~ One copy of each tier per zone

steps.title: Zone A goes dark — failover
steps.body:
Zone A loses power. Health checks fail, the load balancer stops sending traffic there, and the follower in zone B is promoted to leader.

Users in the middle of a request may see an error and retry; within a minute everything runs from zone B.

callout.text: Zone B must have enough spare capacity to carry all the traffic alone. Redundancy you can’t afford to run on is not redundancy.

steps.title: How fast, and how much lost?
steps.body:
Two numbers describe a failover. [[RTO]] (recovery time objective): how long until service is back. [[RPO]] (recovery point objective): how much recent data you can afford to lose.

Async replication means the follower may be a few seconds behind — those writes are gone. Synchronous replication gets RPO to zero, at the cost of slower writes.

callout.text: Decide RTO and RPO with the business first; they determine the design (and the bill).

steps.title: Untested failover doesn’t work
steps.body:
A failover path that never runs quietly rots: a config drifts, a spare is too small, a script has a typo. You find out during the real outage.

So teams break things *on purpose*, in production, during working hours — [[chaos engineering]]. Here a test kills an app server and everyone watches the system cope.

callout.text: Netflix’s Chaos Monkey randomly kills servers every day. Start smaller: a planned game day, one failure at a time.

steps.title: Case: the bug that’s everywhere at once
steps.body:
A new release with a bug goes out to every app server in both zones at the same moment. Every copy crashes on the same request — redundancy doesn’t help when all the copies share the same broken code.

This is the most common cause of real outages: not hardware, but **changes** — code, config, or infrastructure.

callout.text: Identical copies fail identically. A bad change is a correlated failure you inflict on yourself.

changes: + Release v2.4 to all servers at once

steps.title: Canary releases
steps.body:
Roll out in stages instead. First a [[canary]]: one server, or 1% of traffic, gets v2.4. Watch its error rate and latency against the others for a while.

If it looks worse, roll back — only 1% of users were affected, briefly. If it looks good, continue to 10%, 50%, 100%. Many teams also deploy one zone at a time.

callout.text: Feature flags complement this: ship code turned off, then turn it on gradually — and off instantly if needed.

steps.title: Beyond zones: multiple regions
steps.body:
Zones protect against a building failing. A whole **region** can still go down (a regional network or cloud control-plane outage), and it’s far from users on other continents.

Running in two regions with a global DNS or anycast front door lets users go to the nearest healthy region. The hard part is the data: copies across an ocean replicate with ~100 ms of lag.

callout.text: Multi-region is expensive and complex. Most systems are well served by multiple zones in one region plus good backups.

changes: + Global front door routes to the nearest healthy region

steps.title: Recap
steps.body:
• Components in a chain **multiply** their availability.
• Remove **single points of failure** with redundant copies.
• Copies must fail **independently**: spread them across zones.
• Set **RTO/RPO**, and practise failover so it works when needed.
• Most outages are **changes**: roll out with **canaries**.

callout.text: Next up: **Rate Limiting** — protecting the system from too much of the wrong traffic.
